questions.q: In IAM terms, what is a "principal"?
options: Only a human user with a login
Any identity — user, service, or pipeline — that can be granted access
A role with administrator-level privileges
A password or API key used for authentication
questions.explain: A principal is any identity that can be granted access, including people, services like the checkout service, and pipelines like CI/CD runners.

questions.q: Which best describes the principle of least privilege?
options: Granting the minimum access that seems roughly reasonable for a role
Granting admin access by default and narrowing it later if needed
Granting a principal exactly the access its actual job requires, and no more
Granting every principal the same baseline access for consistency
questions.explain: Least privilege means matching access precisely to the real, current job requirement — not "close enough," not admin for convenience, and not inherited from a predecessor's access.

questions.q: Why is a leaked admin credential more dangerous than a leaked read-only credential?
options: Admin credentials use weaker encryption
It has a larger blast radius — more potential damage if compromised or misused
Read-only credentials cannot be leaked at all
There is no meaningful difference in risk
questions.explain: Privilege level determines blast radius. A read-only leak is bounded to viewing data; an admin leak can mean deleted infrastructure or exfiltrated data.

questions.q: At Northbridge Retail, how should the checkout service's access to Key Vault be scoped under least privilege?
options: Full access to every secret in every vault, in case future features need it
Read access to only the specific payment processor secret it actually uses
No access at all, since secrets should never be read programmatically
The same access as the engineer who manages the vault
questions.explain: Least privilege scopes the checkout service to exactly the one secret its current job requires, not the whole vault or broader administrative access.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how do Azure RBAC, AWS IAM, Kubernetes RBAC, and workload identity relate to least privilege?
options: They are unrelated, separate security topics
They are mechanisms for implementing the least-privilege principle in practice
They replace the need for least privilege with automated enforcement
They only apply to human users, not services or pipelines
questions.explain: Least privilege is the guiding principle; the specific identity technologies covered later in the chapter are the tools used to put that principle into practice.
